Schedule follow-up canary plan review on 2026-04-16

summary: Technical deep dive on unexpected accuracy drift after int8 AWQ rollout; discussion covered measurement, per-layer sensitivity, KV cache staleness, batching interactions, routing fallbacks, and onprem/VPC constraints. Agreed to run targeted experiments (layer-probing, seed-controlled runs) and prepare a canary routing plan with sticky KV warmup and precision fallback.
transcript:
Header: 2026-04-08 15:30 UTC, Duration: 73 min
Attendees: Ethan Park, Leah Ortiz, Daniel Wu (Redwood); Sofia Mendes, Ravi Kapoor, Jill Tran (Asteria)
Meeting ID: ff-20260408-asteria-quant-8421

[00:00] Ethan Park: alright folks, good afternoon, thanks for joining. quick check — can everybody hear me?
[00:05] Sofia Mendes: yes, loud and clear. thanks, Ethan.
[00:12] Ethan Park: cool. so, recap from your note — a post-quantize accuracy drift after the int8 AWQ rollout on dedicated. that's what we're here to dig into. Leah, can you start with what you observed in the runbook?
[00:25] Leah Ortiz: yeah, sure. so we saw a ~3.8% drop on our end-to-end qa suite when moving from fp16 baseline to the awq int8 variant. interestingly the token-level loss didn't blow up, it's subtle, it's a few hallucination cases in longer contexts. we also noticed latency improved 1.9x but your throughput variance spiked during bursts.
[00:48] Ravi Kapoor: just to clarify — the rollout was on our dedicated pool in us-east-1, vpc peered. we had batching at 8 on the frontend and the runtime showed kvcache enabled with sticky affinity. maybe there's a warmup issue.
[01:05] Leah Ortiz: right, and the kvcache staleness we measured — some cold-start windows where kv hit-rate dropped to like 20% for certain prompt prefixes. the runtime has a kvcache eviction policy tuned for memory pressure; on bursts we saw evictions that correlated with the drop.
[01:28] Jill Tran: are you suggesting the kv cold starts artificially increase the effective perplexity and cause the model to rely on less accurate tokens?
[01:34] Ethan Park: yeah, that's one hypothesis. another is layerwise quant sensitivity: some middle layers, when quantized, add bias in specific long-range attention patterns. gptq and awq handle per-layer scaling differently.
[01:48] Sofia Mendes: we did a quick AB where we switched to fp8 on the top N layers and kept int8 lower — results were mixed, latency shifted up maybe 10% but the qa metric improved a bit.
[02:05] Leah Ortiz: that matches our expectation: fp8, if implemented with blockwise scaling, reduces quant noise on sensitive layers. awq sometimes uses asymmetric quant and a different rounding; gptq does per-channel correction but slower.
[02:24] Ethan Park: okay let's capture hypotheses — list them: (1) kv cache staleness and warmup causing longer-context hallucinations; (2) layerwise sensitivity where certain attention-mixing layers lose fidelity under pure int8; (3) batching interaction where coalescing pulses cause nonuniform memory scheduling and kernel selection fallbacks — e.g., switching to a fallback codepath that isn't optimized.
[02:47] Ravi Kapoor: can batching actually cause kernel fallback? i thought kernel selection is based on seq-len and hardware.
[02:53] Leah Ortiz: yes, if a coalesced batch pushes max-seqlen or memory footprint above our fast path threshold the runtime may switch to a generic kernel which has slightly different numeric stability. that's rare but seen in bursty traffic.
[03:11] Sofia Mendes: and in our trace we did see an extra 5ms tail in some batches where it goes to a different CUDA kernel, maybe because of kv allocations.
[03:20] Ethan Park: okay good. I want to call out measurement confounds — randomness/seeds, tokenization differences, and eval prompt distribution. did you run deterministic seeds across runs?
[03:31] Sofia Mendes: partially, not fully deterministic across the fleet. we have some nondeterminism from mixed-precision kernels and multi-gpu sharding.
[03:39] Ethan Park: that can mask a 1-2% effect. so step one is an apples-to-apples bisect: fixed seeds, replicate with single-worker, measure per-layer activations and sample-level diffs.
[03:54] Leah Ortiz: agreed. also we should instrument kvcache warmup: track prefix hit-rate per-minute during ramp and tie to sample diffs.
[04:05] Jill Tran: can we also capture the exact binary backtrace when the runtime falls back? our ops team flagged some fallback traces but not full stack.
[04:12] Daniel Wu: yes, we can enable verbose runtime profiling and gather kernel IDs, memory footprint, eviction events. that adds overhead but for a short canary it's fine.
[04:22] Ethan Park: great. let's talk mitigation strategies while we debug. options: 1) precision-mix canary — run awq-int8 in production but route a sticky subset of traffic through a fp8-top-layers variant, 2) routing by prefix — high-value prefixes go to higher precision, 3) sticky-kv warmup — a warmup running in background to pre-populate kvcache for known prefixes, 4) batch-smoothing — enforce max batch seqlen or coalescing window to avoid kernel fallback.
[04:50] Ravi Kapoor: sticky-kv warmup sounds good but on VPC/onprem our ops constraints might not allow a warmup that touches customer data unless we confirm encryption/KMS usage. we need to check compliance.
[05:02] Ethan Park: understood. Redwood's private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs; we can run warmup agents with zero-logging and masked tokens. we'll share the security pattern.
[05:13] Sofia Mendes: how feasible is a per-prefix routing policy? would it increase latency?
[05:18] Leah Ortiz: routing adds a small hop if we call out to policy. but we can implement in the edge tier: tag tokens and route within the same region/pool. the main cost is maintaining model variants and cache coherence.
[05:31] Ethan Park: right, and per-prefix routing requires consistent kvcache affinity or else warmup defeats the purpose. we can do sticky-routing — keep a session pinned to variant for some TTL.
[05:42] Jill Tran: okay, in terms of experiment plan what do you propose? a short checklist would help.
[05:46] Ethan Park: Proposed plan:
- reproducibility runs with fixed seeds and single-worker baseline vs awq-int8 vs gptq-int8 vs fp8-topN.
- per-layer activation diffs and L2 norms to find sensitive layers.
- kvcache warmup simulation: run synthetic warmup for top 200 prefixes and measure hit-rate and metrics.
- routing canary: route 10% of traffic (sticky) to fp8-topN for 72 hrs and compare.

[06:12] Sofia Mendes: will you supply the scripts for layer probing and the config to run deterministic runs?
[06:17] Leah Ortiz: yes, we'll share a reproducibility workbook. it includes a deterministic runner, seed lock, and scripts for dumping layerwise outputs and KV hit traces.
[06:26] Ravi Kapoor: for the VPC firewalling and peering window — our ops can allow a 4-hour maintenance window next Tuesday for the runtime verbose profile run.
[06:35] Ethan Park: perfect, Leah can coordinate with Daniel and Ravi to pick exact times.

--- (20 minute technical section — timestamps approximate) ---
[25:05] Leah Ortiz: quick note — we saw that AWQ's asymmetric quant bins occasionally skew the embedding norms on the first attention layers; it's subtle but shows up when the prompt has nonstandard punctuation and long trailing context.
[25:23] Jill Tran: that's consistent with some of our failing cases — transcripts where users paste long documents with newlines, the model starts hallucinating references.
[25:31] Ethan Park: could tokenizer mismatch be magnifying it? e.g., our tokenizer version vs customer's preprocessing?
[25:36] Sofia Mendes: we upgraded the tokenizer on the client side during the rollout, but the runtime used the older model tokenizer; mismatch might be a real cause.
[25:45] Daniel Wu: oh that's a big find — tokenization diff can change attention patterns and KV index offsets. we should confirm tokenizer hash across stacks.
[25:53] Ethan Park: add to action items: verify tokenizer versions and normalization.

[26:10] Leah Ortiz: re: gptq vs awq — gptq tends to optimize per-channel scales offline, better for accuracy but slower to quantize and not always memory optimal for runtime. AWQ is faster and memory compact but may need per-layer calibration.
[26:29] Ethan Park: if the customer's workflow can't tolerate higher memory, fp8-topN might be a sweet spot — memory-neutral-ish while preserving fidelity on sensitive layers.
[26:39] Jill Tran: what's the overhead of per-layer fp8 mixed precision in inference? do we need new kernels?
[26:44] Leah Ortiz: some fp8 paths use fused kernels or compute in fp16 with fp8 storage; overhead is model-dependent but expect 5-15% latency change vs int8.

[27:05] Sofia Mendes: about evals — our eval suite is 600 prompts but skewed to short-context. i think we need more long-context samples, like 1k-2k tokens, to surface the drift.
[27:17] Ethan Park: agreed. action: customer to supply 500 representative long-context prompts and we'll augment with Redwood curated long-context stress tests.

[27:32] Ravi Kapoor: security check — for any fp8 variant or canary do you create separate model artifacts? how do we manage model versions and rollout policies?
[27:40] Ethan Park: Redwood has model version pinning and rollout policies; we create a variant tag (e.g., model@v2-awq-int8-vs-v2-fp8-topN) and route by model tag. Audit logs record which tokens used which variant.
[27:55] Jill Tran: excellent. do audit logs include per-request tracebacks for kernel fallbacks?
[28:02] Daniel Wu: we can include kernel IDs and fallback flags in trace logs but scrub stack traces for PII.

[28:15] Ethan Park: let's call out measurement instrumentation we will add: deterministic replay, layer L2 diffs, kv hit-rate per prefix, kernel fallback counters, batch seqlen distribution, per-batch memory footprint.
[28:31] Leah Ortiz: and add a micro-experiment: quant-perturbation test — for a small subset of layers, flip quant params (e.g., stochastic rounding on/off) to see sensitivity.
[28:44] Sofia Mendes: sounds good. also can we run a probe comparing awq-int8 with gptq-int8 where we keep everything else equal? i know gptq is slower to generate the quant but for the canary it might be worth it.
[28:57] Ethan Park: yes, Leah will run a parity run.

[29:05] Ethan Park: OK moving towards operational plan — suggested canary routing: 10% sticky traffic mapped by user-session, 72 hours, with rollback triggers: >2% drop in QA metric or >5% increase in hallucination counts, or kernel-fallback rate >0.5%. Are these acceptable?
[29:27] Jill Tran: 2% is tight but acceptable as a threshold; we also want a manual stop if any PII leakage incidents occur.
[29:36] Ravi Kapoor: agreed.

[29:40] Ethan Park: final notes on VPC / onprem: if the customer wants onprem pilot we can ship a private bundle; it requires a support window for kernel binaries and a quick compatibility check with CUDA/drivers. Leah, Daniel, can you outline the preflight checklist?
[29:58] Leah Ortiz: we'll send a checklist: GPU driver versions, CUDA/cuDNN, container runtime, KMS info, allowed egress, and maintenance window. that'll go with the canary plan doc.

[30:12] Sofia Mendes: timeline? how fast can Redwood get the layer-probing scripts and the canary plan?
[30:17] Ethan Park: we'll prioritize — scripts + reproducibility workbook by Friday 2026-04-10, per-layer sensitivity results by 2026-04-12, and canary run targeted for 2026-04-14 to 04-17 depending on peering window.
[30:34] Jill Tran: ops will confirm the peering window by 2026-04-09.

[31:00] Ethan Park: any outstanding questions?
[31:03] Ravi Kapoor: one — how do you handle model drift detection in the console? can we integrate our custom metrics?
[31:09] Daniel Wu: Redwood Console supports custom eval hooks and quality monitors. we can wire up a webhook to push your QA scores and tie alerting to rollout policies.
[31:18] Sofia Mendes: perfect — we'll take that.

[31:24] Ethan Park: cool. recap next steps — i'll send the notes and the workbook; Leah will run layer probes; Daniel will enable verbose profiling during the maintenance window; customer will provide long-context prompts and confirm peering window. any other action?
[31:38] Jill Tran: include tokenizer checksum verification.
[31:41] Ethan Park: done.

[31:45] Sofia Mendes: thanks, team. appreciate the deep dive.
[31:48] Ethan Park: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the documents.

[End of transcript]

Notes: transcript contains minor ASR errors; speaker labels generally accurate but occasional cross-talk and missing punctuation.
